title: Honor your parents
hook: honor, not always obey; care for the old

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabbath, a rest that reaches the servant, the stranger and the donkey. Your line was rest for everyone. Whose load did you lighten? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

The cross, near the end. Jesus looks down and sees his mother standing there, and beside her the disciple he loved. He speaks to her: "Woman, behold thy son!" Then to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And the Gospel adds one plain line: "from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." In his last hours, in pain, Jesus is making arrangements. He's making sure his mother will have a roof and someone to look after her. Today: honor your parents.

The commandment reads: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." Notice the verb. Honor, not obey. Paul does tell children to obey their parents, but the commandment itself speaks to grown adults too, the ones whose parents are getting older and frailer. Some readers hear in the Hebrew word for honor a sense of weight: give your parents weight. Take them seriously. Don't treat them as light. That isn't the same as doing whatever they say. A grown child can disagree, set limits, even keep a safe distance from a parent who does harm, and still refuse contempt. Jesus is sharp on the other side of it, too. In Mark's Gospel he criticizes anyone who declares money a gift dedicated to God so they no longer have to support their own father and mother. Religion is no excuse for leaving the old uncared for. And Paul notices something about this commandment: it's "the first commandment with promise." Honor comes with long days attached. Some readers hear a social promise in that: a people who care for their old will last. Christians practice honor in plain ways: visits, phone calls, hard conversations about care, the patience of telling the same story twice. For those whose parents are gone, or who never had safe ones, some Christians widen it to grandparents, mentors, the elders at the end of the pew. The cross shows the heart of it: even dying, Jesus finds his mother a home.

Here's the practice: call a parent or elder. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a parent, or, if that's too hard or they're gone, an older person who shaped you: a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor. See their face as it is now, not as it was. What are they carrying these days? What would it mean to them to hear from you? Let one small thing to say come to mind. Not a fix. Just weight: I thought of you. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Honor your parents. Giving weight and care to those who raised you, especially as they grow old, even when you can't simply obey.
Your line: honor the old. Today, make the call or send the message, or sit a while with the oldest person you'll see, and let them tell it their way. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians teach this commandment as care for parents throughout life, especially in old age; some churches encourage visiting elderly members and parents, and catechisms extend it to respect for elders and others in authority.

fork.setup: you're the disciple Jesus loved, standing at the cross beside his mother. he says to you, "Behold thy mother!" what do you do?
options: comfort her, then go back to your own life.
take her into your own home from that hour.
leave her with the other women there.
fork.reveal: "from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." honor here is a roof, a table and care.

original.note: Hebrew: honor. The verb that opens Exodus 20:12.

trapdoor: what you thought: honor your parents means always do what they say.
what it means: give them weight and care, especially as they grow old, even when you disagree.
what a scholar hears: the verb is kabbed, honor; Paul calls it the first commandment with promise.
recall: gathering in silence, waiting on God

notes: Mark 7:9–13 (Corban) is paraphrased without naming the Pharisees or scribes, to avoid making them the foil; confirm the paraphrase ('declares money a gift dedicated to God') is accurate.
The Hebrew 'kabbed' and its link to 'weight' (kaved) is attributed to 'some readers'; confirm the attribution is acceptable under the claims rule.
'A grown child can... keep a safe distance from a parent who does harm' is pastoral; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
'A people who care for their old will last' is offered as 'some readers' on the promise of long days; confirm.
